claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in high-entropy FCC/BCC multilayers under sustained loading is governed by interface-mediated dislocation nucleation and accumulation rather than bulk deformation mechanisms.
Accumulated interfacial dislocations eventually cause localized interface decohesion and enhanced slip.
The initial coating consists of alternating nanoscale FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers.
The multilayer retains compositional complexity and intrinsic lattice distortions.
A constant load below the conventional yield stress can be high enough to produce time-dependent deformation.
At room or moderately elevated temperature, thermal activation can support dislocation mobility without causing global phase changes.
FCC/BCC interfaces are preferential sites for dislocation nucleation.
FCC/BCC interfaces are preferential sites for dislocation pile-up.
Preferential interfacial dislocation activity arises from compositional complexity and lattice mismatch.
Sustained loading drives the accumulation of dislocations initiated at high-energy interfaces.
Dislocation pile-ups progressively reduce the local barrier to slip.
Reduced local slip barriers lead to interface decohesion and progressive plastic deformation.
The nanoscale multilayer architecture localizes deformation at or near interfaces instead of distributing it uniformly through the layers.
The undeformed baseline exhibits primarily elastic behavior at low strain, minimal plastic strain, and stable, well-defined interfaces.
Relative to the undeformed baseline, sustained loading will produce progressively increasing plastic strain.
The increasing plastic strain will be localized at multilayer interfaces and observable as interface widening or slip bands.
The proposed mechanism applies when the multilayer is retained with layer thicknesses on the order of 10 nm.
Departures from nanoscale layer dimensions or substantial thermal activation may activate other deformation modes.
Slight compositional modification of interfaces is expected to alter dislocation-nucleation behavior.
